Participants were asked to tie their hair back and remove any clothing items that obscured their face.

During the instruction round, participants were shown how the scales work and it was emphasized that more than one emotion category could be chosen (i.e., that it was possible to experience mixed emotions).
In other words, Dutch participants were more likely to express emotions with higher intensity compared to Japanese participants.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We used PANGEA (Westfall, 2015), a power analysis tool for general ANOVA designs, to determine our sample size. We performed this power calculation based on a mixed model, which included a random intercept per participant. Country, age, and emotion category were entered as fixed factors. Participants were nested within country and age factors. We powered the study to detect the predicted country x age interaction in emotion intensity. Because distinguishing between the two competing predicted patterns also requires examining country differences within each age category, we ensured that the planned sample size provided sufficient precision for these follow-up simple-effects comparisons. Few studies have directly compared emotion production intensity differences between cultural groups, so we decided to estimate our effect size conservatively, grounded on what we would consider a meaningful effect size of interest. Based on our calculations, a sample size of n = 70 (n = 35 children, n = 35 adults) participants at each site (total N = 140) were needed for 95% power to detect a country × age group interaction effect on emotional expression intensity with a small-to-medium effect size (d = 0.4) at the standard error probability of alpha = .05.

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8' to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. Based on our calculations, a sample size of n = 70 (n = 35 children, n = 35 adults) participants at each site (total N = 140) were needed for 95% power to detect a country × age group interaction effect on emotional expression intensity with a small-to-medium effect size (d = 0.4) at the standard error probability of alpha = .05."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p's > .05", Text = "Using a series of independent samples t-tests, it was confirmed that there were also no significant differences in self-report scores between countries on each emotion category, for each age group separately (all p's > .05)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 1 file that software creates by itself, not the authors: R history (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 17 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

This research project was approved by the local Research Ethics Committee at Leiden University (#5086) and the local Research Ethics Committee and Tokyo Woman's Christian University (#A2024-4).
In the Netherlands, on the advice of the ethical review board, we asked adult participants whether they identified as coming from a Western or non-Western background.

live_data_statements: A total of N = 140 participants were recruited.
Finally, since we used visual stimuli, all participants were required to have normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
Children and adults in the Netherlands were recruited online (via social media) and through the Leiden University participant recruitment database.
In Japan, adults were recruited via a local participant database and tested at Tokyo Woman's Christian University.

Children in Japan were recruited and tested as part of a research visit to Miraikan (The National Museum of Emerging Science and Innovation) in addition to laboratory visits at Tokyo Woman's Christian University and Ritsumeikan University in Osaka.
Participants were reimbursed according to the standard rates of each local site.
Participants were nested within country and age factors.

Although participants were made aware that they would be asked to view emotional stimuli, we kept the explicit aims of the study vague and did not divulge which specific emotions we were intending to elicit until the debriefing.
After signing the consent forms, participants were invited to sit in front of a computer screen and fill in some demographic information.
Participants were asked to tie their hair back and remove any clothing items that obscured their face.

During the instruction round, participants were shown how the scales work and it was emphasized that more than one emotion category could be chosen (i.e., that it was possible to experience mixed emotions).
In other words, Dutch participants were more likely to express emotions with higher intensity compared to Japanese participants.
Examination of Figure 1 further confirms this pattern: Dutch participants were generally more expressive than Japanese participants, and children were generally more expressive than adults.
Compared to the Netherlands, Japanese participants were more likely to show higher intensity sadness and fear expressions, and lower intensity disgust and happiness expressions.

Participants were excluded if they gave identical (or near identical, e.g., alternating only between two adjacent values) responses across all trials, such as ratings of 0 or 100 in every item on every video.

After reading the information about the task (or in the case of children, watching an instruction video), providing consent, and filling in some demographic information, participants were shown a subset of n = 16 stimuli from Study 1 to rate in randomized order.
Participants were free to re-watch all videos as many times as they saw fit.
We presented video stimuli using Qualtrics, and participants completed this task using a laptop on a web browser.
A total of N = 552 participants were recruited online via social media, the university research participation platform at Leiden and Tokyo Woman's Christian University, as well as in local schools.
Participants were reimbursed according to the standard rate of the local ethics committee, which differed across sites.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 8 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:8, File = c("Top_5.R", "Pilot_code_RR.R", 
"preprocessing_facereader.R", "preprocessing_script.R", "analysis_script.R", 
"preprocessing_selfreport.R", "inferential_analysis.R", "selfreport_analysis.R"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—", "—", "preprocessing_script.R", 
"—", "preprocessing_selfreport.R", "preprocessing_selfreport.R"
), Basis = c("numeric", "none", "none", "none", "dependency", 
"none", "dependency", "dependency")), row.names = c(NA, -8L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 8 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `nl_adults_raw.csv`, `nl_children_raw.csv`, `jp_adults_raw.csv`, `jp_children_raw.csv`, `selfreport_nl_children.csv`, `selfreport_nl_adults.csv`, `selfreport_jp_children.csv`, `selfreport_jp_adults.csv`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 8 scripts: 2 ran without error, 5 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("Top_5.R", "Pilot_code_RR.R", "preprocessing_facereader.R", 
"preprocessing_script.R", "analysis_script.R", "preprocessing_selfreport.R", 
"inferential_analysis.R", "selfreport_analysis.R"), Outcome = c("errored", 
"errored", "errored", "ran_ok", "timed_out", "errored", "errored", 
"ran_ok"), Detail = c("undefined_variable", "runtime", "runtime", 
"", "timeout", "runtime", "runtime", ""), "Time (s)" = c(50.6, 
97.4, 2.3, 2.9, 300.4, 2.7, 14.8, 4.3)), row.names = c(NA, -8L
), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Top_5.R", "Missing variable" = "time_index", 
    "Defined in" = "(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**2 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: preprocessing_script.R.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("preprocessing_selfreport.R", "preprocessing_script.R"
), "setwd() removed" = c(1L, 1L), "Path(s) it set" = c("(non-literal)", 
"(non-literal)")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

text.text: To what extent are emotions shaped by culture?
Evidence largely comes from adults judging posed emotional expressions, which may not reflect everyday emotional encounters across the lifespan.
Across two pre-registered studies, we examined emotional experience, expression, and perception in Japan and the Netherlands.
In Study 1, 140 participants (children aged 8-12-years-old and adults) watched emotion-evoking videos and reported feelings, while their facial expressions were recorded.
Self-reported emotions were broadly comparable across ages and countries, but Japanese participants displayed less intense facial expressions than Dutch participants, particularly among adults.
In Study 2, 552 Japanese and Dutch child and adult observers judged these expressions.
Regardless of obverse culture, judgments corresponded more closely with Dutch expressers' self-reported emotions, but with Japanese expressers' facial expression intensity.

Thus, broadly comparable emotional experiences may accompany culturally patterned facial expressions, particularly among adults, potentially affecting how closely observers' judgments correspond to expressers' feelings and facial behavior.
Human faces are an omnipresent feature of daily life.
Faces are a significant source of information and capable of a large number of movements that serve clear communicative goals (Niedenthal & Brauer, 2012).
text.formatted: Faces are a significant source of information and capable of a large number of movements that serve clear communicative goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Niedenthal & Brauer, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: These facial movements can be used to make inferences about others' mental states, including emotions (Keltner & Haidt, 1999; Krumhuber et al., 2023).
text.formatted: These facial movements can be used to make inferences about others' mental states, including emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Keltner & Haidt, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Krumhuber et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Given the importance of emotional expressions for daily social life, this raises a deceptively simple question -to what extent are emotional experiences, expressions, and perception shared across cultural bounds (see; Cowen et al., 2024; Durán & Fernández-Dols, 2021; Ekman, 1970; Elfenbein & Ambady, 2002; Russell, 1994)?
text.formatted: Given the importance of emotional expressions for daily social life, this raises a deceptively simple question -to what extent are emotional experiences, expressions, and perception shared across cultural bounds (see; <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Cowen et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Durán & Fernández-Dols, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Ekman, 1970;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Elfenbein & Ambady, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Russell, 1994)</ref>?

text.text: Many studies have examined how culture influences the way people perceive emotions (Beaupré & Hess, 2005; Bryant & Barrett, 2008; Cordaro et al., 2018a; Ducci et al., 1982; Ekman et al., 1969; Ekman, 1970; Elfenbein et al., 2007a; Elfenbein & Ambady, 2002; Hutchison et al., 2018; Matsumoto & Ekman, 1989) and these studies have often been used as evidence to make claims about the universality of emotion expressions (Barrett et al., 2019; Cordaro et al., 2018b; Scherer et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Many studies have examined how culture influences the way people perceive emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Beaupré & Hess, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bryant & Barrett, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cordaro et al., 2018a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Ducci et al., 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Ekman et al., 1969;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Ekman, 1970;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Elfenbein et al., 2007a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Elfenbein & Ambady, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Hutchison et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Matsumoto & Ekman, 1989</ref>) and these studies have often been used as evidence to make claims about the universality of emotion expressions <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Barrett et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Cordaro et al., 2018b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Scherer et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: However, this literature has several key limitations.

First, it has focused almost exclusively on emotion perception, with far less attention devoted to how emotions are expressed in different cultures (but see; Cordaro et al., 2018; Cowen et al., 2024; Matsumoto et al., 2008; Naab & Russell, 2007; Tsai et al., 2002).
text.formatted: First, it has focused almost exclusively on emotion perception, with far less attention devoted to how emotions are expressed in different cultures (but see; <ref type="bibr">Cordaro et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Cowen et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Matsumoto et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Naab & Russell, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Tsai et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Second, emotion perception studies, often use highly posed expressions derived from adult expressers, raising questions about how well these stimuli reflect emotional behavior as it is seen in real life (Cong et al., 2025a; Krumhuber et al., 2021a Krumhuber et al., , 2021b;; Riddell et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Second, emotion perception studies, often use highly posed expressions derived from adult expressers, raising questions about how well these stimuli reflect emotional behavior as it is seen in real life <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cong et al., 2025a;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Krumhuber et al., 2021a</ref> <ref type="bibr">Krumhuber et al., , 2021b;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Riddell et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Third, because posed expressions may not reflect emotions that expressers were actually experiencing, studies rarely assess the correspondence between observers' judgements and expressers' reported subjective experiences (Barrett et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Third, because posed expressions may not reflect emotions that expressers were actually experiencing, studies rarely assess the correspondence between observers' judgements and expressers' reported subjective experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Barrett et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, most cross-cultural studies have focused on adults' judgments, while children have been considered significantly less, limiting our understanding of the role of the developmental processes within a culture may influence how emotions are felt, expressed, and perceived.
Direct evidence for cross-cultural variation in emotion production remains comparatively scarce.

One study found that Japanese, North American and European adults' emotions to evocative videos were found to be expressed using similar facial muscles, however, Japanese participants' facial expressions tended to be less intense than those in North America and Europe overall (Cowen et al., 2024). Cordaro and colleagues (2018) identified 22 international "core patterns" of facial and body behavior associated with emotions that occurred above chance across different cultures.
text.formatted: One study found that Japanese, North American and European adults' emotions to evocative videos were found to be expressed using similar facial muscles, however, Japanese participants' facial expressions tended to be less intense than those in North America and Europe overall <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Cowen et al., 2024)</ref>. <ref type="bibr">Cordaro and colleagues (2018)</ref> identified 22 international "core patterns" of facial and body behavior associated with emotions that occurred above chance across different cultures.

text.text: However, 19 of the 22 emotions also showed some notable cultural differences (e.g., in awe and pride).
As such, these limited studies suggest both cross-cultural commonality and divergence in expression production (Elfenbein et al., 2007a).
text.formatted: As such, these limited studies suggest both cross-cultural commonality and divergence in expression production <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Elfenbein et al., 2007a)</ref>.

text.text: The comparably limited studies in infants and children point to a similar pattern.
For example, Camras and colleagues (2007) found high cross-cultural similarities in Japanese, Chinese and North American infants' facial expressions during arm restraint and stranger approach.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr">Camras and colleagues (2007)</ref> found high cross-cultural similarities in Japanese, Chinese and North American infants' facial expressions during arm restraint and stranger approach.

text.text: Beyond infancy, dyads of mothers and preschool-aged children in the United States showed higher levels of emotional expressivity compared to dyads in Thailand (Rochanavibhata & Marian, 2023).
text.formatted: Beyond infancy, dyads of mothers and preschool-aged children in the United States showed higher levels of emotional expressivity compared to dyads in Thailand <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Rochanavibhata & Marian, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Further evidence suggests that White American children are more likely to display happiness, sadness, and anger in response to emotion-eliciting events compared to Korean and Asian-American children (Louie et al., 2013 (Louie et al., , 2015)).
text.formatted: Further evidence suggests that White American children are more likely to display happiness, sadness, and anger in response to emotion-eliciting events compared to Korean and Asian-American children <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Louie et al., 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Louie et al., , 2015))</ref>.

text.text: These mixed findings leave open whether cross-cultural differences in emotional expressions are already evident early in childhood, when social learning and display rules have not been fully established yet (Clément & Dukes, 2017; Saarni, 1979), and whether these differences become more pronounced with age.
text.formatted: These mixed findings leave open whether cross-cultural differences in emotional expressions are already evident early in childhood, when social learning and display rules have not been fully established yet <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Clément & Dukes, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Saarni, 1979)</ref>, and whether these differences become more pronounced with age.

text.text: This uncertainty also complicates the inferences from studies on cross-cultural perception of emotion.

An in-group advantage (i.e., more accurate perception of stimuli from one's own culture) may reflect cultural variation in the expression being judged, variation in the perceiver's emotion knowledge, or a combination of these.

Adult empirical studies and a meta-analysis have found evidence for an ingroup advantage for basic emotions (Beaupré & Hess, 2005; Elfenbein & Ambady, 2002; Matsumoto et al., 2009; Scherer et al., 2011), with further evidence that these advantages extend to other discrete emotions (e.g., serenity and shame; Elfenbein et al., 2007b), vocalizations (Sauter et al., 2010), and body movements (Parkinson et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Adult empirical studies and a meta-analysis have found evidence for an ingroup advantage for basic emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Beaupré & Hess, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Elfenbein & Ambady, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Matsumoto et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Scherer et al., 2011)</ref>, with further evidence that these advantages extend to other discrete emotions (e.g., serenity and shame; <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Elfenbein et al., 2007b)</ref>, vocalizations <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Sauter et al., 2010)</ref>, and body movements <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Parkinson et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, a recent study has challenged these earlier findings, suggesting that the in-group advantage disappears when accounting for different cultures in both expressers and observers (Cong et al., 2025b).
text.formatted: However, a recent study has challenged these earlier findings, suggesting that the in-group advantage disappears when accounting for different cultures in both expressers and observers <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cong et al., 2025b)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, it remains unclear whether these adult findings generalize to children.

The more limited literature on cross-cultural emotion perception in children presents a mixed pattern, with the magnitude of the advantage seemingly depending on the modality (e.g., faces vs. voices) and increasing with age (Chronaki et al., 2018; Kawahara et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The more limited literature on cross-cultural emotion perception in children presents a mixed pattern, with the magnitude of the advantage seemingly depending on the modality (e.g., faces vs. voices) and increasing with age <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chronaki et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Kawahara et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: One study found evidence of an ingroup advantage in their sample of 3-to-7-year-old children: White American children were generally more accurate in recognizing emotions of White American compared to Black American facial expressions (Tuminello & Davidson, 2011).
text.formatted: One study found evidence of an ingroup advantage in their sample of 3-to-7-year-old children: White American children were generally more accurate in recognizing emotions of White American compared to Black American facial expressions <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Tuminello & Davidson, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, while one study found that South Asian Canadian children, but not White Canadian children, were more proficient at recognizing the emotions in own-race faces compared to other-race faces (Segal et al., 2019), another study found no ingroup advantage (Glanville & Nowicki, 2002).
text.formatted: Furthermore, while one study found that South Asian Canadian children, but not White Canadian children, were more proficient at recognizing the emotions in own-race faces compared to other-race faces <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Segal et al., 2019)</ref>, another study found no ingroup advantage <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Glanville & Nowicki, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: To investigate cross-cultural differences in emotion experience, expression, and perception, we conducted two preregistered studies with children aged 8-12 years and adults from Japan and the Netherlands.

Japan and the Netherlands were selected because they differ starkly in their cultural makeup and sociocultural norms (Hofstede, 1984 (Hofstede, , 2011;; Matsumoto et al., 2008), and previous research suggests cross-cultural differences in emotional expression between these countries (Cowen et al., 2021; Kawahara et al., 2021; Matsumoto & Ekman, 1989).
text.formatted: Japan and the Netherlands were selected because they differ starkly in their cultural makeup and sociocultural norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hofstede, 1984</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Hofstede, , 2011;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Matsumoto et al., 2008)</ref>, and previous research suggests cross-cultural differences in emotional expression between these countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cowen et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Kawahara et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Matsumoto & Ekman, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: In Study 1, participants watched videos validated to elicit happiness, sadness, fear, and disgust across cultures, reported their emotional experiences, while they were video recorded.
We examined cultural and age-group differences in the intensity of facial expressions, while considering self-reported emotional experience.
We tested whether Dutch-Japanese differences in facial-expression intensity varied by age group.
Larger cultural differences among adults than children would be consistent with greater cultural differentiation in expression with age.
In Study 2, independent Japanese and Dutch child and adult observers judged a subset of the expressions recorded in Study 1.

We examined the correspondence between observers' judgements and expressers' self-reported emotions, as well as between observers' judgements and observable facial movements -indexed using automated coding of facial action units.
We tested whether observers' judgements were more closely aligned with own-culture than other-culture expressers' self-reported emotions and observable facial behaviour.
Additionally, we examined whether any own-culture advantage across these metrics differed between children and adults.
We did not formulate emotion-specific hypotheses; primary analyses examined patterns across the elicited emotions.

This research project was approved by the local Research Ethics Committees at Leiden University (#5086) and Tokyo Woman's Christian University (#A2024-4).
A total of N = 140 participants were recruited.
Children were required to be between the ages of 8 and 12-years-old, and adults between 18-40-years-old.
A breakdown of participant demographic information is displayed in Table 1.
text.formatted: A breakdown of participant demographic information is displayed in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: In addition to age requirements, we required participants to be fluent in Dutch (for the Dutch wing of the study) and Japanese (for the Japanese wing of the study).
Finally, since we used visual stimuli, all participants were required to have normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
In Japan, both 100% of adults and 100% of children's parents identified as ethnic Japanese.

In the Netherlands, on the advice of the ethical review board, we asked participants (or in the case of children, their parents) whether they identified as coming from a Western or non-Western background.
Of our Dutch participants, 97.3% of adults identified as Western, and 80.5% of children's parents identified as Western.

We had complete self-report data for all participants (except n = 1 Japanese adult), however, due to video processing issues, as well as some participants who obscured their face during the viewing of the stimuli, there were some missing data for the facial expression portion of the analysis.
In Japan, n = 5 adults and in the Netherlands n = 1 child and n = 1 adult were missing from the analysis with facial emotional expressions.
We used PANGEA (Westfall, 2015), a power analysis tool for general ANOVA designs, to determine our sample size.
text.formatted: We used PANGEA <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Westfall, 2015)</ref>, a power analysis tool for general ANOVA designs, to determine our sample size.

text.text: We performed this power calculation based on a mixed model, which included a random intercept per participant.
Country, age, and emotion category were entered as fixed factors.
Participants were nested within country and age factors.
We powered the study to detect the predicted country x age interaction in emotion intensity.

Because distinguishing between the two competing predicted patterns also requires examining country differences within each age category, we ensured that the planned sample size provided sufficient precision for these follow-up simple-effects comparisons.

Few studies have directly compared emotion production intensity differences between cultural groups, so we decided to estimate our effect size conservatively, grounded on what we would consider a meaningful effect size of interest.

Based on our calculations, a sample size of n = 70 (n = 35 children, n = 35 adults) participants at each site (total N = 140) were needed for 95% power to detect a country × age group interaction effect on emotional expression intensity with a small-to-medium effect size (d = 0.4) at the standard error probability of alpha = .05.

The present study had a factorial design with two between-subjects' factors: age of the expresser (2 levels: adults, children) and country of the expresser (2 levels: Netherlands, Japan) and one within-subjects' factor (which as only of exploratory interest): target emotion of the stimulus (4 levels: happiness, sadness, disgust and fear).
As indicated, we examined whether emotional facial expression intensity across different distinct emotions differed across both cultural and age groups.
In this study, we performed an emotion-induction task using video stimuli designed to elicit specific emotions across different cultural contexts.
This technique has been used in previous studies with children (Khan et al., 2019) and adults (Schaefer et al., 2010).
text.formatted: This technique has been used in previous studies with children <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Khan et al., 2019)</ref> and adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Schaefer et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Although participants were made aware that they would be asked to view emotional stimuli, we kept the explicit aims of the study vague and did not divulge which specific emotions we were intending to elicit until the debriefing.
After signing the consent forms, participants were invited to sit in front of a computer screen and fill in some demographic information.
Participants were asked to tie their hair back and remove any clothing items that obscured their face.
For adult participants, we asked for their: age, gender, country of birth, cultural background (in the Netherlands:
Western/Non-Western/Other/Prefer Not to Say; in Japan: Japanese/Non-Japanese) household income, and highest level of education.
For child participants, we asked their parents for their child's: age, gender, country of birth.
Additionally, we asked parents to report their own highest level of education, cultural background and household income in the same way as adult participants.
For participants not born in the Netherlands or Japan, we asked how long they have lived in the Netherlands or Japan (to control for this if necessary).
Both age groups were given written instructions for task, in which the various scales were explained.
For children specifically, the researcher read the instructions verbally seated next to the child, so the child had the opportunity to ask for clarification.

During the instruction round, participants were shown how the scales work and it was emphasized that more than one emotion category could be chosen (i.e., that it was possible to experience mixed emotions).
For children, the definition of each of the emotion terms was explained to ensure they understood their meaning.
The researcher also practiced sliding the scales with the child.
After the instructions, the emotion induction task begun.
The researcher (and, in the case of children, the parent) were asked to leave the room.
After this, a series of ten short (max 4-minute) video clips, drawn from a series of movies and YouTube videos, were displayed in randomized order.
We use different stimuli for children and adults to ensure that the stimuli were age appropriate.

These stimuli were drawn from various databases and have been used in previous works to induce happiness, sadness, disgust, fear and neutrality (Gross & Levenson, 1995; Khan et al., 2019; Sato et al., 2007; Schaefer et al., 2010; Zupan & Eskritt, 2020).
text.formatted: These stimuli were drawn from various databases and have been used in previous works to induce happiness, sadness, disgust, fear and neutrality <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Gross & Levenson, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Khan et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Sato et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Schaefer et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Zupan & Eskritt, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: To maximize the chances of inducing emotions, each participant viewed two videos intended to induce each of the four emotion categories (plus two neutral stimuli).
For a full list of stimuli see Supplementary Materials 1.

After the participant viewed each video, they were asked to indicate how they felt during the viewing by indicating their emotional state on a sliding scale with a list of emotion words in their native language (e.g., "During this video, I felt happy/sad/disgust/fear/neutral [0-100]") (see Supplementary Materials 1 for translations into Dutch and Japanese).
After viewing all the stimuli, the participant was asked to provide permission for their video stimuli to be used in the follow-up emotion recognition project and the experiment was concluded.
We used a Logitech C920 HD webcam and ring lamp to record individuals during the viewing of the induction videos.
We filmed each participant's face and upper body as they sat in front of the screen and watch each video.
Participants wore a white t-shirt to keep the recordings as standardized as possible.
The webcam was placed on the monitor, at approximately 30cm distance from the participant.
Stimuli were displayed and self-report ratings collected using a survey displayed with Qualtrics on a web browser.
Videos were derived from popular movies and YouTube clips, ranging from approximately 30 seconds to 4 minutes.
We displayed all stimuli to adults with subtitles, and audio dubbing for children (since many of the youngest children were still learning to read).

Since the induction stimuli used in this study varied in length, and most emotions were likely to occur only at specific points throughout the displayed stimulus material, we trimmed the webcam recordings of participants at pre-specified times such that they were all the same length (20 seconds -see Stimulus List in Supplementary Materials 1).

To standardize the stimuli and maximize the chance of these trimmed videos containing facial expressions of emotion but limiting researcher degrees of freedom by manually selecting a unique expression apex for each participant, we pre-specified the to-be-trimmed time portions of each expresser's reaction video.

These trim points are indicated in Supplementary Materials 1 and represent 5-seconds before and 15-seconds after the point in the induction video that was most intense and, therefore, likely to be maximally emotion-evoking.

For example, we showed an excerpt from the film Forrest Gump to adults to induce happiness, and we trimmed each of the reaction videos to cover the moments before and after the scene in the clip in which the protagonist is reunited with his lover.
In this way, each participant's reaction reflected the same moment in the induction stimulus, allowing us to make standardized comparisons across stimuli and participants.

To check whether the induction videos induced the intended target emotions, we examined participants' self-report scores on each of the induction videos to determine whether the participants reported feeling the intended target emotion.

As per our preregistration, a video was considered "successful" in inducing the target emotion if participants reported, at a group level, significantly higher scores on the target emotion compared to neutral.
For example, if the video was intended to induce feelings of happiness, the induction was considered successful if participants reported feeling significantly more happiness than neutral.
Since we used different stimuli for children and adults, we used separate models for each age group and collapsed scores across cultures.
Induction success for each age group was tested using a Gaussian linear mixed model using the glmmTMB package (Brooks et al., 2017 ) in R Studio (Citing RStudio, 2023).
text.formatted: Induction success for each age group was tested using a Gaussian linear mixed model using the glmmTMB package <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Brooks et al., 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr">) in R Studio (Citing RStudio, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we used the difference between participants' self-report scores on the target emotion and their scores on neutral as the dependent variable, and video type as a factor (eight levels: corresponding to each of the two videos for each of the four target emotions).
We allowed intercepts to vary across participants.
Since we used sum coding for the video type factor, a significant positive intercept would be indicative of a grand mean significantly greater than zero.

To examine whether the means were significantly above zero across videos, we inspected the marginal means of the model output to ascertain whether the estimated mean was positive and its 95% CI did not span zero, using the emmeans package (Lenth et al., 2019).
text.formatted: To examine whether the means were significantly above zero across videos, we inspected the marginal means of the model output to ascertain whether the estimated mean was positive and its 95% CI did not span zero, using the emmeans package <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Lenth et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This would suggest that the stimulus induced the target emotion to a significantly greater extent than it induced neutrality.
After checking the manipulation success of the task, the next step was to derive the facial expression intensity scores based on observable facial action units (AUs).
To do this, we process all the 20-second trimmed recordings through an automatic facial expression recognition software package FaceReader (Noldus, 2014).
text.formatted: To do this, we process all the 20-second trimmed recordings through an automatic facial expression recognition software package FaceReader <ref type="bibr">(Noldus, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: FaceReader classifies facial expressions on the basis of an artificial neural network, trained on manually coded images based on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) (Ekman & Friesen, 1978).
text.formatted: FaceReader classifies facial expressions on the basis of an artificial neural network, trained on manually coded images based on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Ekman & Friesen, 1978)</ref>.

text.text: It classified our four emotions of interest: happiness, sadness, fear and disgust on the basis of the activation of the facial action units associated with each emotion's "prototypical" display (e.g., the emotion sadness is constituted by activation of AUs 1 + 4 + 15, corresponding to a raising of the inner brow, lowering of the brow and down turning of the lip corners).
For each frame of the video, the software gives an intensity score for each of the above listed emotions between 0-1 at a 10Hz frame rate.
We used FaceReader's general facial expression model for Dutch participants, and the East-Asian model for Japanese participants.
For our analyses, we examined the FaceReader intensity scores for the target emotion specifically, extracting its peak intensity (i.e., maximum, or apex) within each 20-second clip.

Because group differences in target-emotion intensity scores could reflect crosscultural variation in the broader configuration of facial action units recruited during emotional expression, rather than differences in the prototypical expression of target emotion alone, we additionally conducted an exploratory control analysis of peak-frame AU profiles.
We pooled the two emotion-eliciting videos and identified the single frame with the highest total activity across 19 FaceReader-derived AUs for each participant separately.
Within this peak frame, the 19 AUs were ranked from most to least active.
We then summarised, within each group, the percentage of participants for whom each AU appeared among the five most prominent AUs for that emotion.

This approach allowed us to characterise the relative configuration of facial activity at participants' peak-expression frames, rather than the absolute intensity or presence of individual AUs and is decribed in detail in Supplementary Materials 2.

While this analysis revealed some specific differences -most clearly, a lower relative prominence of AU6 (cheek raiser) and AU12 zygomaticus major in Japanese adults' happiness displays -the broader AU profiles showed substantial overlap between groups and generally good correspondence with the theoretically expected emotion displays (Figure S3).
text.formatted: While this analysis revealed some specific differences -most clearly, a lower relative prominence of AU6 (cheek raiser) and AU12 zygomaticus major in Japanese adults' happiness displays -the broader AU profiles showed substantial overlap between groups and generally good correspondence with the theoretically expected emotion displays (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S3</ref>).

text.text: Together, this pattern indicates that the cross-cultural differences in facial-expression intensity reported above are unlikely to be attributable solely to cultural differences in the broader sets of AUs recruited.
As in the manipulation check, we performed all our analyses using the glmmTMB function.
Although we did not pre-register this, we firstly looked at the relationship between age and culture on participants' self-reported emotions.
Here, we performed a beta linear mixed model with sum coded age of the expresser (child vs. adult), country of the expresser (Netherlands vs.
Japan), as well as their interaction, as predictors of self-reported emotional state, for the target emotion specifically.

In these analyses, we opted for a Beta-regression as the scores were proportional (0-100, later converted to 0 > score > 1) as this analysis is highly suited to proportional data (Smithson & Verkuilen, 2006).
text.formatted: In these analyses, we opted for a Beta-regression as the scores were proportional (0-100, later converted to 0 > score > 1) as this analysis is highly suited to proportional data <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Smithson & Verkuilen, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Since Beta-regressions cannot be used for the analysis of proportions equal to zero or one, we scaled the scores according to the formula (1.1): where N is the sample size (Smithson & Verkuilen, 2006, pp. 55).
text.formatted: Since Beta-regressions cannot be used for the analysis of proportions equal to zero or one, we scaled the scores according to the formula (1.1): where N is the sample size <ref type="bibr">(Smithson & Verkuilen, 2006, pp. 55)</ref>.

text.text: As above, we allowed intercepts to vary across participants.
Next, as per our pre-registration, we performed an additional beta linear mixed model on FaceReader facial emotion maximum intensity scores, with the same fixed effects structure as above.
We included a random intercept per participant and nested this within the factors country and age.

For ease of interpretation, we followed up all models using the Type 3 ANOVA function from the car package (Fox et al., 2019) and used the emmeans package (Lenth et al., 2019) to contrast the marginal effects.

ANOVAs, and the output of the full regression models in the Supplementary Materials 2.
Importantly, for all beta linear mixed models, we took the exponent of the model coefficients to interpret the estimates at the odds ratio level.

Additionally, in the case of any nonsignificant findings, we also followed up our frequentist tests with Bayesian analyses using the brms function in R Studio, and used the Bayes factor, using bayesfactor_parameters function in the bayestestR package (Makowski et al., 2019), to quantify evidence for and against the null hypothesis.

text.text: We specified the same model structure as that specified above, and used weakly informative priors for fixed effects (M = 0, SD = 1) and the intercept (M = 0, SD =1).
In our exploratory analyses, we were interested in examining patterns of responding across specific emotion categories.
First, we examined whether there were any differences in the intensity of participants facial expressions for each emotion category using an additional Beta linear mixed model.
Here, we included age group, country, and target emotion as fixed effects, allowing the intercepts to vary per participant.
Additionally, we were also interested in exploring the relationship between participants' self-reported emotions and their corresponding facial expressions.
Specifically, we aimed to determine whether this relationship varied across emotion categories, age groups, and countries.

To examine this, we created a generalized linear mixed model, including a random intercept for each participant and allowing slopes to vary within participants for the effect of self-report scores on the target emotion, for each emotion category.
All random effects were specified as uncorrelated for computational efficiency.

Firstly, we examined whether the emotion induction task resulted in participants reporting having experienced the target emotion significantly more than the amount that they reported feeling neutral, separately for both children and adults.
Full model outputs are available in Supplementary Materials 2.
In the model on children's self-report, the intercept, representing the grand mean of all the videos displayed, was positive and significant, β = 28.75, 95% CI = [20.27, 37.22], p < .001 (Table S1).

text.text: This suggests that the stimuli displayed evoked more emotions than neutrality.

When homing in on the specific emotion effects for each video in the child group, the marginal means revealed that all stimuli (except both "Fear" videos) resulted in the induction of the target emotion significantly more than neutral (Table S2).

text.text: In the model on adult's self-report, the intercept was positive and significant, β = 51.72, 95% CI = [45.03, 58.39], p < .001 (Table S3) and adults, therefore, reported feeling the target emotion significantly more than neutral across all emotion stimuli (Table S4).

text.text: As such, it appears that all stimuli, except the fearful videos in childhood, resulted in the induction of the intended target emotions.

Although the fear stimuli that we displayed to children did not seem to result in the induction of self-reported fear significantly above neutral, the means were positive (indicating an induction in the correct direction), so we decided to nonetheless still include these data in our eventual models in the interest of parsimony, as well as in line with our pre-registered analysis.
Next, we examined whether there were significant differences across age and countries on participants' self-report ratings of emotions, within one model.
The beta linear mixed model revealed no differences across both countries and age groups on self-reported emotion scores, χ 2 (1) = 0.01, p = .930; χ 2 (1) = 2.01, p = .156, respectively.
We followed up this test with a Bayesian beta linear mixed model, retaining the same structure, to assess evidence for the null hypothesis (Table S6).
text.formatted: We followed up this test with a Bayesian beta linear mixed model, retaining the same structure, to assess evidence for the null hypothesis (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S6</ref>).

text.text: This revealed anecdotal evidence for a lack of difference in self-report across age, OR = 0.77, 95% CI = [0.53-1.12], BF10 = 0.48; and moderate evidence for a lack of difference across countries on self-reported emotion scores, OR = 1.02, 95% CI = [0.71-1.49], BF10 = 0.19.
Ultimately, these analyses suggest that participants of different ages and countries did not report feeling emotions of differing intensities during the presentation of our stimuli overall.

Following our pre-registration, we then examined whether there were significant differences across both age groups and countries in terms of participants' facial expression intensity on the target emotion.
The model, displayed in Table 4, revealed a significant main effect of country, χ 2 (1) = 13.12, p < .001.
text.formatted: The model, displayed in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">4</ref>, revealed a significant main effect of country, χ 2 (1) = 13.12, p < .001.

text.text: Examination of the contrasts revealed that the odds of Japanese individuals displaying facial emotions with greater intensity were 0.76 times the odds of individuals in the Netherlands, OR = 0.76, 95% CI = [0.66, 0.88].
In other words, Dutch participants were more likely to express emotions with higher intensity compared to Japanese participants.

Additionally, we found a significant main effect of age, χ 2 (1) = 5.46, p = .019; with the odds of an adult displaying a higher intensity facial expression 0.84 times the odds of the child group, OR = 0.84, 95% CI = [0.73, 0.97].
In other words, children were more likely to show higher intensity facial expressions, on average, compared to adults.
Examination of Figure 1 further confirms this pattern: Dutch participants were generally more expressive than Japanese participants, and children were generally more expressive than adults.
text.formatted: Examination of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref> further confirms this pattern: Dutch participants were generally more expressive than Japanese participants, and children were generally more expressive than adults.

text.text: In line with our hypotheses, we further zoomed in on the extent to which children and adults of different cultures differed in their emotion intensity scores by examining the marginal means.
As pre-registered, it was the between-culture differences within each age group that were of primary importance.
Although the interaction between age and country was not significant (Table 4), we proceeded with the planned contrasts to directly test our competing pattern of results.
text.formatted: Although the interaction between age and country was not significant (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">4</ref>), we proceeded with the planned contrasts to directly test our competing pattern of results.

text.text: The results revealed a significant difference between Japanese and Dutch adults in terms of facial emotion intensity, OR = 1.41, 95% CI = [1.15, 1.74], p = .001.
This suggests that Dutch adults were more expressive than Japanese adults.
However, no significant differences could be found between Japanese and Dutch children on facial emotion intensity, OR = 1.22, 95% CI = [1.00, 1.48], p = .053.

This was confirmed by examination of the contrasts in a follow-up Bayesian independent samples t-test, which revealed moderate evidence for a lack of a difference between Dutch (M = 0.26, SD = 0.30) and Japanese (M = 0.26, SD = 0.30) children on facial emotion intensity, BF10 = 0.22.

Therefore, the difference in emotional expression intensity between Japan and the Netherlands was mostly driven by the differences between adults, not children. on the density map represent regions where data points are more concentrated.

In addition to our pre-registered analyses, we also sought to explore any differences in emotional expressivity across age and culture, when also considering specific emotions.
To this end, we performed an additional beta linear mixed model, including age group, country, and emotion category (as well as their interactions) as fixed effects.
The full regression output and analysis can be found in Supplementary Material 2.
The model revealed a significant interaction effect between emotion category and age, as well as an interaction effect between emotion category and country.
When zooming in on the emotion category by age contrasts, the results revealed that children displayed significantly more intense fear and happiness compared to adults.
The emotion category by country contrasts revealed significant cultural differences across all emotion categories.
Compared to the Netherlands, Japanese participants were more likely to show higher intensity sadness and fear expressions, and lower intensity disgust and happiness expressions.
The full results of this model are presented in Figure S2 and Table S13.
text.formatted: The full results of this model are presented in Figure <ref type="figure">S2</ref> and Table <ref type="table">S13</ref>.

text.text: Next, we aimed to quantify whether the relation between participants' self-reported emotion and corresponding facial expression varied across emotion categories, age groups, and countries.
The details of the analysis can be found in Supplementary Materials 2.

Importantly, the analyses revealed a significant self-report score × emotion category × country interaction effect, such that, in the Netherlands, both children and adults displayed more intense facial expressions of happiness as their self-reported happiness increased, compared to Japanese children and adults.
In Japan, higher self-reported happiness was associated with more intense expressions of happiness for children only, whereas for adults this relation was non-significant.
In addition, for Dutch adults, higher self-reported sadness was associated with more intense corresponding facial expressions of sadness, though the equivalent relation for fear was non-significant.
Japanese children additionally showed a positive association between self-reported and expressed disgust.
Interestingly, while Japanese children and adults generally displayed high levels of sadness, this was not related to their self-report scores (Figure 3).
text.formatted: Interestingly, while Japanese children and adults generally displayed high levels of sadness, this was not related to their self-report scores (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: The relationship between self-reported emotion and facial expressions was non-significant across all other combinations of emotion, age group and country (Table S14).
text.formatted: The relationship between self-reported emotion and facial expressions was non-significant across all other combinations of emotion, age group and country (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S14</ref>).

text.text: These findings indicate that Dutch adults' experiences of sadness and happiness (but not fear or disgust) were informative of their corresponding facial expressions, but this was not the case for Japanese adults for any emotion assessed.

Dutch and Japanese children showed a broadly similar pattern for happiness, with self-reported happiness predictive of facial expressions of happiness in both groups; Japanese children additionally showed this correspondence for disgust.
Intensity, Split Across Age Group and Country, for Each Emotion Category Separately
We screened all participants' response data for evidence of inattentive or invalid responding prior to analysis.

Participants were excluded if they gave identical (or near identical, e.g., alternating only between two adjacent values) responses across all trials, such as ratings of 0 or 100 in every item on every video.
This resulted in the exclusion of n = 10 participants, all of whom were Dutch children.

Note that screening was not conducted blind to participant nationality; however, the exclusion criterion (identical or near-identical responses across all trials) was applied uniformly and did not involve subjective judgment.

Since we used Bayesian methods of statistical inference for our emotion perception analyses, we pre-registered a stopping rule of collecting data until we reached strong evidence (BF > 10) for either the alternative or null hypothesis of primary interest -namely, a three-way interaction between expresser country, observer country, and observer age group (reflecting an in-group advantage moderated by age), which in turn required comparable evidence for the underlying two-way interaction between expresser and observer country.

text.text: We originally pre-registered a target of n = 200 per group (N = 800 total).

Due to resource constraints, particularly in recruiting child participants, we did not reach this target in both child groups (n = 52 Japanese children; n = 105 Dutch children; see Table 5 for full sample characteristics).

text.text: Because Bayes factors can be interpreted at any sample size without requiring a fixed pre-specified sample size, we were still able to draw valid conclusions about the strength of evidence given the data collected, even though the target evidential threshold may not have been reached in the child groups.

This study had a factorial design with two between-subjects' factors: age of the observer (2 levels: adults, children), country of the observer (2 levels: Netherlands, Japan) and three within-subjects' factors: age of the expresser (2 levels: adults vs. children), country of the expresser (2 levels: Netherlands, Japan), and target emotion category of the expresser (4 levels: happiness, sadness, disgust and fear), the last being only of exploratory interest.

As indicated, we examined the effects of these variables on two separate agreement indices: the absolute distance between observers' ratings and expressers' self-reported emotion, and the absolute distance between observers' ratings and facial expression intensity, as computed by the software FaceReader (Noldus, Wageningen).

In this study, we asked an independent group of same-age observers as the participants in Study 1 to view the processed video stimuli (see processing details below in "Materials") and rate these according to which emotion(s) they believed the Study 1 participant (i.e., the expresser) experienced.
We indicated that children could complete the task in the presence of their parents, but that parents should not interfere or help their children in any way.

After reading the information about the task (or in the case of children, watching an instruction video), providing consent, and filling in some demographic information, participants were shown a subset of n = 16 stimuli from Study 1 to rate in randomized order.
These stimuli were fully balanced for culture, emotion and age, such that each participant saw one child and one adult from each culture for each of the four emotion categories.
Participants were free to re-watch all videos as many times as they saw fit.

Participants used the same rating system as was used in Study 1: a series of sliding scales with a list of emotion words presented in their native language, (e.g., "The person in this video clip feels happy/sad/fear/disgust/neutral [1-100]").
Additionally, they were asked to indicate the expresser's valence and arousal levels on the same scale as Study 1.
After participants rated all stimuli, they were provided with a plain-language debriefing with information about the task and our aims.
The experiment took approximately 25 minutes for children, and 15 minutes for adults.
We only used the 20-second trimmed videos from Study 1 for which we had obtained consent from participants (and in the case of children, their parents).
We defined a-priori a series of eligibility criteria.
To achieve a fully balanced design, we required a pool of n = 32 unique videos per emotion category, split evenly across both countries and age groups (total = 128 unique stimuli).
All videos in which the self-reported experience of the target emotion was higher than 10 for the target emotion were considered eligible for inclusion.

Using a series of independent samples t-tests, it was confirmed that there were also no significant differences in self-report scores between countries on each emotion category, for each age group separately (all p's > .05).
text.formatted: Using a series of independent samples t-tests, it was confirmed that there were also no significant differences in self-report scores between countries on each emotion category, for each age group separately (all p's > .05).

text.text: We assessed videos chronologically according to the date that Study 1 participants came to the lab, up until we reached the total maximum number of stimuli needed.
The emotion perception experiment itself was conducted entirely online.
We presented video stimuli using Qualtrics, and participants completed this task using a laptop on a web browser.

We operationalized emotion perception agreement by examining the absolute distance between: a) self-and observer-reported emotional experience and b) facial expression intensity (as derived by FaceReader) and observer-reported emotion scores on the target emotion specifically.

For example, if a stimulus presented to an expresser in Study 1 was intended to induce the emotion "happiness", we calculated a self-and observer-reported emotion agreement score by comparing both values on the "happiness" scale alone (not considering the values on other emotion scales).
The same premise applied for calculation of the agreement scores between observer-reports and facial expression intensity scores.
For facial expression analyses, we took the peak intensity score of each emotion as calculated by
FaceReader during the 20-second recording and multiplied this by 100.
This gave a rating of the intensity of each expressed emotion on the same scale as the observer-reported scores (0-100).
We implemented all models using the brms package in R Studio unless otherwise specified.

Since agreement scores were bounded (values could not be higher than 100 or less than 0), first transformed the data according to the recommendations of Smithson and Verkuilen (2006), in the same way as Study 1, which resulted in a dependent variable that included no zeros or ones.
text.formatted: Since agreement scores were bounded (values could not be higher than 100 or less than 0), first transformed the data according to the recommendations of <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Smithson and Verkuilen (2006)</ref>, in the same way as Study 1, which resulted in a dependent variable that included no zeros or ones.

text.text: Then, using sum-to-zero coding, we fit two Bayesian regression models, one model for each outcome: absolute distance between: a) self-and observerreported emotional experience and b) facial expression intensity (as derived by FaceReader) and observer-reported emotion scores on the target emotion specifically.
These models used Beta error distributions that predicted agreement by observer age, observer country, expresser age, expresser country.

In addition to these main effects, we included an additional three-way (observer age * observer country * expresser country) interaction term to test our hypothesis regarding the influence of both culture and age on emotion recognition.

In an additional series of exploratory models, we re-ran our main models but included the effect of emotion category as an additional interaction term to delineate whether the effects in our preregistered analyses held when considering the potentially influential effect of emotion category.

In all models, we included random intercepts for each observer (nested in age category) and expresser ID (to account for potential differences in the ease in which observers could judge specific expressers).
We specified Gaussian priors for all fixed effects.
In all cases, for the intercept, we specified a weakly informative prior with M = 0 and SD = 5.
For all other fixed effects, we specify a conservative prior with M = 0 and SD = 1, placing most probability mass on small effects.
For all variance parameters, we retain default priors.
To inspect model fit, we examined Rhat and ESS values, as well as by visual inspection of the trace diagnostics and posterior predictive check plots.
We report coefficients (b) on the logit scale alongside exponentiated coefficients, exp(b), to facilitate interpretation.
Exponentiated main-effect coefficients represent odds ratios, whereas exponentiated interaction coefficients represent ratios of odds ratios.
To examine the robustness of our findings, we performed a sensitivity analysis on all our models by adjusting our priors and examining whether the interpretation of our results changed.

We performed three separate analyses -each containing either a narrow, wider, or widest prior and inspected each outcome to determine whether the adjustment of the priors had putative impact on the interpretation of our findings.

Additionally, posterior predictive checks indicated inadequate fit of the preregistered observer-self-report discrepancy model, with the model showed higher density near zero than one than in the observed data.
We therefore fitted a zero-one-inflated beta sensitivity model to accommodate exact zeros and ones without boundary correction.
Predictive fit improved, although some small discrepancies remained.
The results of this analysis are presented in Supplementary Materials 3 and did not indicate major effects of prior specification on the interpretation of our findings.
In the first pre-registered analysis, we examined the correspondence between observers' ratings of expressers' emotions and expressers' self-reported emotional experiences.

We modelled the absolute distance between self-reported and observer-reported emotion scores, such that lower values indicated closer correspondence and higher values indicated greater discrepancy (see Table 6 for overview of these scores collapsed across participant groups).

text.text: To this end, we conducted a Bayesian beta mixed effects model which tested the effects of age group, country of the observer, and the country of the expresser on the absolute agreement between the self-and observer-reported emotion scores.
The model, displayed in Table 7, revealed a credible effect of expresser country and observer country.

Most critically, we found no evidence for a cultural in-group advantage on emotion perception, supported by examination of the Bayes factors for our competing hypotheses.

The first, which posited an effect of culture in the absence of an effect of age (i.e., an observer × expresser country interaction), revealed very strong evidence for the absence of an effect BF01 = 48.26.

The second, which posited an effect of culture moderated by age (i.e., an observer country × expresser country × observer age interaction), revealed similarly very strong evidence for the absence of an effect BF01 = 65.1.

In the second pre-registered analysis, we examined the correspondence between observers' emotion ratings and observed facial expression intensity for the target emotion.
As in the preceding analysis, we modelled the absolute difference between the two measures, such that lower values indicated closer correspondence and higher values indicated greater discrepancy.
We fitted a Bayesian beta mixed-effects model with the same fixed-effects structure as in the self-report analysis.
The model, displayed in Table 8, similarly revealed a main effect of expresser country, b = -0.15, 95% CI = [-0.30, -0.00], exp(b) = 0.86, but in the opposite direction.

text.text: Across observer groups, the difference between observers' emotion ratings and FaceReader target-emotion intensity scores was larger for Dutch than Japanese expressers.
In other words, observers' ratings corresponded more closely with the emotion intensity observable in Japanese compared to Dutch facial expressions.
Examination of the key interaction effects of interest revealed that this was independent of the age and cultural group of the observer.
Regarding the two-way (observer × expresser culture) interaction, that could reveal an ingroup advantage, the Bayes factor revealed very strong evidence for the absence of an effect, BF01 = 66.84.
Furthermore, regarding the three-way (observer country × expresser country × observer age) interaction, the Bayes factor also revealed very strong for the absence of an effect, BF10 = 73.4.
Therefore, we found evidence of no in-group advantage in how emotions were judged relative to their facial expression intensity.
Taken together, observers' ratings aligned less closely with Japanese expressers' selfreported emotions, but more closely with the emotion intensity observable in Japanese facial
