Taken together, although these analyses identified a small number of emotion-specific patterns -and very few patterns additionally qualified by observer country and age -these effects generally did not suggest evidence of an in-group advantage in emotion perception overall.
There has been much debate in the literature regarding the extent to which expressions of emotion are shared across cultures.
However, this research has been limited by a primary focus on adult emotion perception, the use of posed stimuli, and little consideration of people's experience of emotions.

Across two preregistered studies, we addressed these limitations and examined the experience, expression, and perception of happiness, sadness, fear, and disgust among children and adults in Japan and the Netherlands.

In Study 1, we found that self-reported emotional experiences were broadly similar across countries, whereas Dutch expressers displayed more intense facial expressions that more closely matched their own subjectively reported feelings than Japanese expressers.

In Study 2, observers' ratings across cultures corresponded less closely with Japanese than Dutch expressers' self-reported emotions, but more closely with Japanese than Dutch expressers' facial-expression intensity.
Neither pattern varied by observers' country, providing evidence for a lack of cultural in-group advantage.

Regarding the relation between emotional experience and expression, the cultural difference in facial-expression intensity is notable because it emerged despite broadly comparable self-reported emotional experiences across countries.

The finding that Dutch participants generally displayed higher intensity facial expressions compared to Japanese participants is in line with some previous studies that found that Japanese (and other East Asian) participants typically display lower intensity facial expression compared to Western participants (e.g., Cowen et al., 2024; Schouten et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The finding that Dutch participants generally displayed higher intensity facial expressions compared to Japanese participants is in line with some previous studies that found that Japanese (and other East Asian) participants typically display lower intensity facial expression compared to Western participants (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Cowen et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Schouten et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We further extend this body of work through our inclusion of a developmental sample.

Our analyses revealed that significant differences in expression intensity between Dutch and Japanese participants was mainly driven by differences between Dutch and Japanese adults' displayed facial expression intensity, while we found no differences in facial emotion intensity between children in the Netherlands and Japan.

This may suggest that Japanese children, unlike Japanese adults, may not have fully internalized the display rules for emotions in their culture, which dictate generally low expressivity of emotions (Ekman et al., 1969; Matsumoto et al., 2008; Schouten et al., 2020) and expressed emotions with similar intensity as Dutch children.
text.formatted: This may suggest that Japanese children, unlike Japanese adults, may not have fully internalized the display rules for emotions in their culture, which dictate generally low expressivity of emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Ekman et al., 1969;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Matsumoto et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Schouten et al., 2020)</ref> and expressed emotions with similar intensity as Dutch children.

text.text: An additional interesting finding regarding cultural differences was that the associations between self-reported experience and visible facial emotional expression intensity was generally weaker for Japanese adults.
This implies that these participants not only show lower intensity emotional expressions, but also that these expressions were less reflective of their internal states.
This is perhaps also attributable to the display rules that more strongly regulate emotional expressions in Eastern Asian cultures (Safdar et al., 2009; Song et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This is perhaps also attributable to the display rules that more strongly regulate emotional expressions in Eastern Asian cultures <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Safdar et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Song et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: It is perhaps no surprise then that, in Study 2, observers' ratings corresponded less closely with Japanese than Dutch expressers' self-reported emotions.
However, conversely, observers' ratings corresponded more closely with the facial-expression intensity of Japanese than Dutch expressers.

This implies that observers could better judge what Dutch participants felt based on their displayed emotions in the videos, likely because Dutch participants' selfreported feelings were more often associated with their displayed facial expression intensity.
For Dutch expressers, the face seemed to provide a relatively more informative cue to selfreported emotional experience.
For Japanese expressers, by contrast, observers' ratings corresponded more closely to facial-expression intensity but less closely to self-reported experience.
Thus, Japanese facial behaviour may have provided a relatively consistent cue to the emotion visibly expressed, while serving a less direct cue to expressers' reported inner experiences.
While patterns across Study 2 depended on the expresser's country, there was no effect of the observers' country, providing evidence for a lack of cultural in-group advantage in emotion perception.
This result may sound surprising given a previous meta-analysis which found evidence for this (Elfenbein & Ambady, 2002).
text.formatted: This result may sound surprising given a previous meta-analysis which found evidence for this <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Elfenbein & Ambady, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: However, a more recent study by Cong and colleagues (2025b) challenged these findings, suggesting that when balanced designs are used (in which observers of both countries judge expressers of both countries) these effects may disappear.

text.text: Our study, which similarly used a balanced design, is consistent with this more recent study.

Together, the findings of the two studies suggest that similar emotional experiences across cultures may be accompanied by differences in the intensity of facial emotional expressions, particularly among adults, with consequences for how closely others can infer emotions from the face.
There are a few limitations in our design worth mentioning.

Firstly, we provided participants with emotion labels when providing their self-reported emotional state and this constrained their responses to several emotions (e.g., happiness, sadness, fear, disgust), framing the emotion space as containing discrete categories.
As such, future research may consider using experience sampling or free-response questions to allow participants to indicate their emotional state in their own words.
Another key limitation of our study was that we were unable to adequately induce self-reported fear in our child sample in Study 1.
However, we observed prototypical fear facial expressions in children, that were significantly more intense than those of adults.
This could suggest that children may not have wanted to report feeling afraid, even if they did so, given the negative associations with this emotion state at this age (Dadds et al., 1998).
text.formatted: This could suggest that children may not have wanted to report feeling afraid, even if they did so, given the negative associations with this emotion state at this age <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Dadds et al., 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, we should be careful when drawing conclusions about this emotion in children specifically.

Future studies could consider the use of physiological recordings (e.g., heart rate, electrodermal activity) to better characterize the participants' emotional responding and to better tease apart where any differences in emotional responding lie (Mauss et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Future studies could consider the use of physiological recordings (e.g., heart rate, electrodermal activity) to better characterize the participants' emotional responding and to better tease apart where any differences in emotional responding lie <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Mauss et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: A final limitation concerns the Study 2 observer sample sizes.
Owing to resource constraints, we did not reach the preregistered stopping rule of 200 participants in each child observer group.

Although this shortfall does not invalidate the Bayesian interpretation of the primary analyses, it warrants caution when interpreting the results, and particularly the exploratory, emotion-specific findings.
Across two preregistered studies, we jointly examined emotional experience, facial expression, and emotion perception in Japanese and Dutch children and adults.

Despite broadly similar self-reported emotional intensity across countries, Japanese participants displayed less intense facial expressions than Dutch participants, with cultural differences most pronounced among adults.
Observers from both countries showed closer agreement with Dutch expressers' reported emotional experiences, but closer agreement with Japanese expressers' facial-expression intensity.
Neither pattern depended on observer country, providing no evidence for a cultural in-group advantage.

By linking expression production with perception and subjective feelings, our findings suggest that cultural differences in emotion involve not only how strongly feelings are expressed in the face, but also how closely observers' judgements correspond to those feelings and facial expressions.
This highlights the need for psychological theories of emotion and social understanding to account for culturally variable associations among emotion experience, expression, and perception.

text.text: This research project was approved by the local Research Ethics Committee at Leiden University (#5086) and the local Research Ethics Committee and Tokyo Woman's Christian University (#A2024-4).
A total of N = 552 participants were recruited online via social media, the university research participation platform at Leiden and Tokyo Woman's Christian University, as well as in local schools.
Children were required to be between the ages of 8 and 12-years-old, and adults between 18-40-years-old.
A breakdown of participant demographic information is displayed in Table 5.
text.formatted: A breakdown of participant demographic information is displayed in Table <ref type="table">5</ref>.

text.text: In addition to age requirements, we required participants to be fluent in Dutch (for the Dutch wing of the study) and Japanese (for the Japanese wing of the study).
Finally, since we used visual stimuli, all participants were required to have normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
In Japan, 99% of adults and 100% of children's parents identified as Japanese.
In the Netherlands, on the advice of the ethical review board, we asked adult participants whether they identified as coming from a Western or non-Western background.
Of our Dutch participants, 94% of adults identified as Western.
Collecting demographic information from Dutch children (or their parents) proved difficult, and, as such, we did not collect this data.
Participants were reimbursed according to the standard rate of the local ethics committee, which differed across sites.
Dutch children were entered into a raffle to win one of 25 small toy prizes (value approximately €10).
Dutch adults were reimbursed according to the standard rate at Leiden University: research credits or €4,25.
The parents of Japanese children received a 1500¥ gift card for their child's participation, while Japanese adults received a 600¥ gift card.
As in Study 1, as an additional exploratory analysis, we examined whether correspondence between observer ratings and the comparison measures differed across emotion categories.

We fitted Bayesian beta mixed-effects models that extended the preregistered models by including emotion category and its interactions with observer age group, observer country, and expresser country.
Detailed model output and estimated marginal contrasts are reported in Supplementary Materials 3 (Tables S1, S2, and S3).
text.formatted: Detailed model output and estimated marginal contrasts are reported in Supplementary Materials 3 (Tables <ref type="table">S1</ref>, <ref type="table">S2</ref>, and <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: Because both outcomes indexed absolute differences, we describe the findings in terms of closer or poorer correspondence.
Observers' ratings matched Japanese expressers' self-reported emotions less closely than Dutch expressers' self-reported emotions for fear, among both child and adult observers.
Among adults, the same pattern emerged for disgust and sadness.

The disgust and sadness patterns, however, were qualified by observer country: the poorer correspondence with Japanese expressers' self-reports was most apparent among Dutch adult observers for disgust, but among Japanese adult observers for sadness.
When observer ratings were compared with the emotion intensity observable in facial expressions, the overall pattern was reversed.
For disgust and happiness, both child and adult observers' ratings corresponded more closely with the emotion intensity observable in Japanese than Dutch facial expressions.
Adult observers also showed this pattern for fear.

These effects were broadly similar across observer countries, although the stronger correspondence between observer ratings and Japanese facial-expression intensity for happiness was especially pronounced among Japanese observers.
These inconsistent findings leave open not only whether an in-group advantage emerges during development, but also what such an advantage would represent.

Previous attempts cannot distinguish whether cross-cultural differences in apparent recognition perception arise from differences in expressers' emotional experiences, their facial expressions, observers' interpretations, or a combination of these factors.
Addressing this issue requires studies that jointly assess elicited expressions, expressers' reported experiences, and observers' judgements in children and adults from different cultural contexts.
